11: ## V2 Mode Rules
12: 
13: Modes describe how arguments are expected to be instantiated when a relation is called.
14: 
15: Modes are separate from ordinary types and separate from determinism.
16: 
17: ### Parameter modes
18: 
19: ```cosmos
20: rel p(In Number x, Out Number y)
21: ```
22: 
23: Supported modes:
24: 
25: ```text
26: In
27:     Argument must be sufficiently instantiated before the call.
28: 
29: Out
30:     Argument is expected to be produced by the call.
31: 
32: InOut
33:     Argument may already contain information and may be further
34:     instantiated by the call.
35: ```
36: 
37: Internally, modes may be represented compactly as:
38: 
39: ```text
40: In      +
41: Out     -
42: InOut   ?
43: ```
44: 
45: Example:
46: 
47: ```cosmos
48: rel concat(In A, In B, Out C)
49: ```
50: 
51: may be represented internally as:
52: 
53: ```text
54: concat(+A,+B,-C)
55: ```
56: 
57: The source language should normally use `In`, `Out`, and `InOut`.
58: 
59: ---
60: 
61: ### Modes precede types
62: 
63: The mode appears before the parameter type:
64: 
65: ```cosmos
66: rel p(In Any x)
67: rel get(In Table t, In Any key, Out Any value)
68: rel has(In List l, InOut Any x)
69: ```
70: 
71: If no mode is declared, the parameter has no explicit mode constraint.
72: 
73: Mode inference may still determine an effective mode for checking or optimization.
74: 
75: ---
76: 
77: ### Multiple modes
78: 
79: A relation may support more than one valid calling mode.
80: 
81: For example:
82: 
83: ```text
84: concat:
85:     (In, In, Out)
86:     (In, Out, In)
87:     (Out, In, In)
88:     (Out, Out, In)
89: ```
90: 
91: These are distinct mode signatures of the same relation.
92: 
93: The compiler should select a compatible mode from the known instantiation state at the call site.
94: 
95: If no declared mode is compatible, report a mode error.
96: 
97: ---
98: 
99: ### Determinism
100: 
101: Determinism describes the possible number of successful solutions for a particular mode.
102: 
103: ```text
104: det
105:     Exactly one solution.
106: 
107: semidet
108:     Zero or one solution.
109: 
110: multi
111:     One or more solutions.
112: 
113: nondet
114:     Zero or more solutions.
115: ```
116: 
117: Determinism belongs to a mode signature rather than to the relation name alone.
118: 
119: Example:
120: 
121: ```text
122: has(In list, In value)   semidet
123: has(In list, Out value)  multi
124: ```
125: 
126: The same relation can therefore have different determinism depending on how it is called.
127: 
128: ---
129: 
130: ### Standard mode examples
131: 
132: # Note: this is user documentation/illustratory. Do not hard-implement modes for those relations.
133: 
134: #### `size`
135: 
136: ```text
137: size(In collection, Out size)  det
138: size(In collection, In size)   semidet
139: ```
140: 
141: Surface syntax:
142: 
143: ```cosmos
144: n = #list
145: ```
146: 
147: may lower to:
148: 
149: ```text
150: size(list,n)
151: ```
152: 
153: ---
154: 
155: #### `concat`
156: 
157: ```text
158: concat(In A, In B, Out C)    det
159: concat(In A, Out B, In C)    semidet
160: concat(Out A, In B, In C)    semidet
161: concat(Out A, Out B, In C)   multi
162: ```
163: 
164: The first mode represents ordinary concatenation.
165: 
166: The last mode represents relational decomposition.
167: 
168: ---
169: 
170: #### `get`
171: 
172: For:
173: 
174: ```cosmos
175: x = table[key]
176: ```
177: 
178: with logical form:
179: 
180: ```text
181: get(table,key,x)
182: ```
183: 
184: useful modes include:
185: 
186: ```text
187: get(In collection, In key, Out value)    semidet
188: get(In collection, Out key, Out value)   multi
189: get(In collection, Out key, In value)    multi
190: ```
191: 
192: If invalid indexing is defined to throw rather than fail, the first mode may instead be treated as `det` with an exceptional case.
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: #### `has`
197: 
198: ```cosmos
199: x in l
200: ```
201: 
202: lowers to:
203: 
204: ```text
205: has(l,x)
206: ```
207: 
208: Useful modes:
209: 
210: ```text
211: has(In collection, In value)   semidet
212: has(In collection, Out value)  multi
213: ```
214: 
215: A compact declaration may therefore use:
216: 
217: ```cosmos
218: rel has(In Collection l, InOut Any x)
219: ```
220: 
221: while retaining the more precise mode signatures internally.
222: 
223: ---
224: 
225: ### Mode checking
226: 
227: Mode checking tracks whether variables are sufficiently instantiated at each program point.
228: 
229: Example:
230: 
231: ```cosmos
232: rel p(Out Number x)
233:     x=2
234: ```
235: 
236: After the call:
237: 
238: ```cosmos
239: p(x)
240: ```
241: 
242: `x` is considered produced/instantiated according to the selected mode.
243: 
244: An `In` parameter cannot be supplied with a value that is insufficiently instantiated for that mode.
245: 
246: ---
247: 
248: ### `function`
249: 
250: `function` introduces a stronger callable contract than an ordinary `rel`.
251: 
252: A function is expected to execute deterministically and not accidentally expose logical failure or multiple solutions.
253: 
254: Example:
255: 
256: ```cosmos
257: function wait()
258:     print("> ") and io.read(x)
259: 
260:     if(x="halt")
261:         c::halt()
262: ```
263: 
264: Here:
265: 
266: ```text
267: print(...)      det
268: io.read(...)    det
269: x="halt"        semidet
270: ```
271: 
272: The equality is valid as the condition of `if`, because failure is expected and consumed by the conditional.
273: 
274: This is potentially invalid:
275: 
276: ```cosmos
277: function wait()
278:     print("> ")
279:     io.read(x)
280:     x="halt"
281:     c::halt()
282: ```
283: 
284: because `x="halt"` can fail and therefore makes the function itself potentially fail.
285: 
286: ---
287: 
288: ### Failure-consuming contexts
289: 
290: A `semidet` or `nondet` goal may appear where its failure is intentionally handled.
291: 
292: Examples include:
293: 
294: ```cosmos
295: if(p(x))
296:     ...
297: 
298: not p(x)
299: 
300: once p(x)
301: 
302: p(x) or q(x)
303: ```
304: 
305: A function-mode checker should distinguish these contexts from an unguarded potentially failing goal.
306: 
307: The rule is not specific to equality.
308: 
309: It applies to any goal whose determinism permits failure.
310: 
311: ---
312: 
313: ### Void operations
314: 
315: `Void` is not an argument mode.
316: 
317: It describes an operation whose result is used only for its effect.
318: 
319: For example:
320: 
321: ```text
322: print(In Any) : det, void
323: ```
324: 
325: A void operation may still be deterministic or nondeterministic independently of being void.
326: 
327: Thus:
328: 
329: ```text
330: Mode          In / Out / InOut
331: Determinism   det / semidet / multi / nondet
332: Result use    value-producing / void
333: ```
334: 
335: are separate properties.
336: 
337: ---
338: 
339: ## V2 protocol / Interface Rules
340: 
341: A protocol describes structural requirements on a value and may optionally define behavioral constraints.
342: 
343: Example:
344: 
345: ```cosmos
346: protocol(Moving,{
347:     Number x
348: 
349:     rel p(x)
350:         x>2
351: })
352: ```
353: 
354: A protocol may contain:
355: 
356: - required fields;
357: - required relation/function members;
358: - type requirements;
359: - mode requirements;
360: - optional behavioral constraints.
361: 
362: ---
363: 
364: ### Structural members
365: 
366: A declaration without an implementation body is an ordinary interface requirement.
367: 
368: Example:
369: 
370: ```cosmos
371: protocol(Moving,{
372:     Number x
373:     rel move(In Number dx, In Number dy)
374: })
375: ```
376: 
377: A conforming value must provide:
378: 
379: ```text
380: x
381:     compatible with Number
382: 
383: move
384:     callable with a compatible relation signature
385: ```
386: 
387: No runtime behavior is specified beyond the signature.
388: 
389: ---
390: 
391: ### Behavioral relation constraints
392: 
393: A protocol relation with a body describes a constraint on the corresponding implementation.
394: 
395: Example:
396: 
397: ```cosmos
398: protocol(Moving,{
399:     Number x
400: 
401:     rel p(x)
402:         x>2
403: })
404: ```
405: 
406: means that a conforming object must provide a compatible `p`, and successful calls to that `p` must satisfy:
407: 
408: ```text
409: x > 2
410: ```
411: 
412: The body is therefore a contract/constraint, not the implementation of `p`.
413: 
414: ---
415: 
416: ### Runtime contract checking
417: 
418: Given:
419: 
420: ```cosmos
421: ship.p(x)
422: ```
423: 
424: and protocol constraint:
425: 
426: ```cosmos
427: rel p(x)
428:     x>2
429: ```
430: 
431: debug-mode execution may behave conceptually as:
432: 
433: ```text
434: call ship.p(x)
435: then check x>2
436: ```
437: 
438: If `ship.p(x)` succeeds but the protocol constraint fails, this is a protocol violation.
439: 
440: The protocol body should not be interpreted as relation equality such as:
441: 
442: ```text
443: p(x) = ship.p(x)
444: ```
445: 
446: Instead it constrains the successful behavior of the implementation.
447: 
448: ---
449: 
450: ### Static versus runtime checking
451: 
452: protocol conformance should be checked statically when enough information is available.
453: 
454: For example:
455: 
456: ```cosmos
457: Moving ship = expression
458: ```
459: 
460: requires the compiler to verify that `expression` conforms to `Moving` as far as statically possible.
461: 
462: If some requirement cannot be established statically, a runtime check may be retained.
463: 
464: Behavioral constraints may be checked in debug/runtime-contract mode even when the structural interface is statically known.
465: 
466: ---
467: 
468: ### `is`
469: 
470: ```cosmos
471: ship is Moving
472: ```
473: 
474: is a conformance predicate.
475: 
476: Its ordinary mode is:
477: 
478: ```text
479: is(In value, In type/protocol) : semidet
480: ```
481: 
482: It succeeds when the value conforms to the requested nominal type or protocol.
483: 
484: Example:
485: 
486: ```cosmos
487: if(ship is Moving)
488:     ship.move(1,0)
489: ```
490: 
491: If conformance is already proven statically, the compiler may simplify:
492: 
493: ```cosmos
494: ship is Moving
495: ```
496: 
497: to `true`.
498: 
499: Otherwise it emits the required runtime check.
500: 
501: ---
502: 
503: ### Nominal type checks
504: 
505: `is` may also check nominal types:
506: 
507: ```cosmos
508: ship is Ship
509: ```
510: 
511: For values introduced through:
512: 
513: ```cosmos
514: ship = new Ship(1,2)
515: ```
516: 
517: the compiler already knows:
518: 
519: ```text
520: ship : Ship
521: ```
522: 
523: and may eliminate the check.
524: 
525: Nominal type identity and protocol conformance are distinct:
526: 
527: ```text
528: ship is Ship
529:     nominal/type identity or declared conformance
530: 
531: ship is Moving
532:     protocol/interface conformance
533: ```
534: 
535: A value may satisfy a protocol without having that protocol as its nominal type.
536: 
537: ---
538: 
539: ### protocol compatibility
540: 
541: A value conforms structurally when every required member exists with a compatible signature.
542: 
543: For fields:
544: 
545: ```text
546: Number x
547: ```
548: 
549: the actual `x` must have a compatible type.
550: 
551: For relations:
552: 
553: ```cosmos
554: rel p(In Number x, Out Number y)
555: ```
556: 
557: the implementation must support a compatible mode and type signature.
558: 
559: Its determinism must also be compatible with the protocol promise.
560: 
561: For example, an implementation declared `nondet` should not satisfy a protocol member that promises `det`.
562: 
563: ---
564: 
565: ### Mode compatibility in protocols
566: 
567: Modes are part of a callable protocol member's interface.
568: 
569: Example:
570: 
571: ```cosmos
572: protocol(Source,{
573:     rel read(In String path, Out String text)
574: })

592:

650: ## V2 `new` / Object Rules
651: 
652: ### `new`
653: 
654: ```cosmos
655: ship = new Ship(1,2)
656: ```
657: 
658: means:
659: 
660: ```text
661: 1. resolve Ship
662: 2. require Ship.new
663: 3. call Ship.new(ship,1,2)
664: 4. bind/type-check ship as Ship
665: ```
666: 
667: Conceptually:
668: 
669: ```text
670: x = new T(args...)
671: →
672: T.new(x,args...)
673: type(x) = T
674: ```
675: 
676: `new` does not implicitly invoke `object.create`.
677: 
678: `new` does not itself enable prototype inheritance.

680: If `T.new` does not exist, `new T(...)` is a compile-time error.

683: 
684: ### Explicit object creation
685: 
686: Prototype-oriented programming remains opt-in through `object.create`.

688: Example:
689: 
690: ```cosmos
691: Ship ship = object.create(Ship,{
692:     x=1
693:     y=2
694: })
695: ```
696: 
697: This explicitly creates an object using `Ship` as its prototype/template while also requiring the resulting value to type-check as `Ship`.
698: 
699: The type annotation itself does not create the object.

701: ---
702: 
703: ### Typed binding
704: 
705: ```cosmos
706: Ship ship = expression
707: ```
708: 
709: means:
710: 
711: ```text
712: evaluate expression
713: check expression against Ship
714: bind ship : Ship
715: ```
716: 
717: This may be used independently of `new` or `object.create`.

720: 
721: ### Separation
722: 
723: ```text
724: new T(...)
725:     constructor call + T type information
726: 
727: T x = Expr
728:     static type requirement
729: 
730: x is T
731:     runtime-capable semidet conformance check
732: 
733: object.create(...)
734:     explicit prototype/object construction
735: 
736: protocol(...)
737:     structural and optional behavioral interface
738: ```
739: 
740: Object/prototype semantics remain optional and are not implied merely by using types, protocols, or `new`.

743: ## V2 Clarifications
744: 
745: ### Callable categories
746: 
747: `rel`, `function`, and `void` are callable categories.
748: 
749: ```text
750: rel
751:     Relational. May fail and/or produce multiple solutions.
752: 
753: function
754:     Non-relational/deterministic-style callable. Intended to behave as a single-result operation.
755: 
756: void
757:     Non-relational callable whose result is not logically consumed.
758:     Used primarily for host/internal/IO/side-effect operations.
759: ```
760: 
761: Examples:
762: 
763: ```cosmos
764: void read(...)
765:     ...
766: 
767: io.read=read
768: ```
769: 
770: ```cosmos
771: void halt()
772:     c::halt()
773: ```
774: 
775: For mode checking, `void` is treated as effectively safe in a `function` body.
776: 
777: Thus:
778: 
779: ```cosmos
780: function wait()
781:     print("> ")
782:     io.read(x)
783: 
784:     if(x="halt")
785:         os.halt()
786: ```
787: 
788: is valid even though the underlying implementation of `io.read` or `os.halt` may terminate, throw, perform IO, or otherwise behave outside ordinary relational semantics.
789: 
790: `void` therefore means more than “returns no value.” It marks a callable as outside ordinary relational success/failure reasoning.
791: 
792: For current purposes:
793: 
794: ```text
795: void ≈ det for function-mode analysis
796: ```
797: 
798: although an implementation may technically be described as `semidet, void` or may terminate exceptionally.
799: 
800: The checker should not infer relational failure from such host/non-relational behavior.
801: 
802: ---
803: 
804: ## Modes
805: 
806: Modes remain properties of relation parameters:
807: 
808: ```text
809: In
810: Out
811: InOut
812: ```
813: 
814: They may be expressed using the existing type/declaration syntax rather than introducing a separate signature syntax.
815: 
816: For example:
817: 
818: ```cosmos
819: rel move(In Number dx, In Number dy)
820:     true
821: ```
822: 
823: describes both parameter types and modes.
824: 
825: Equivalent type/interface information may also be expressed separately:
826: 
827: ```cosmos
828: Relation In In move
829: Relation Number Number move
830: ```
831: 
832: The first declaration describes modes:
833: 
834: ```text
835: move(In, In)
836: ```
837: 
838: The second describes ordinary parameter types:
839: 
840: ```text
841: move(Number, Number)
842: ```
843: 
844: Together they describe:
845: 
846: ```text
847: move(In Number, In Number)
848: ```
849: 
850: This avoids requiring additional protocol-specific syntax.
851: 
852: ---
853: 
854: ## Determinism
855: 
856: Determinism is relevant primarily to relational callables:
857: 
858: ```text
859: det
860: semidet
861: multi
862: nondet
863: ```
864: 
865: Examples:
866: 
867: ```text
868: concat(In, In, Out)   det
869: has(In, In)            semidet
870: has(In, Out)           multi
871: ```
872: 
873: `function` and `void` participate differently in checking:
874: 
875: ```text
876: rel
877:     ordinary relational determinism applies
878: 
879: function
880:     expected to behave as a non-failing/non-branching callable,
881:     except where failure is explicitly consumed
882: 
883: void
884:     treated as non-relational for function-flow checking
885: ```
886: 
887: Thus a `void` operation is allowed directly inside a `function`:
888: 
889: ```cosmos
890: function f()
891:     print("x")
892:     io.read(x)
893: ```
894: 
895: without requiring those operations to be modeled as ordinary logical goals.
896: 
897: ---
898: 
899: ## Function failure checking
900: 
901: Potentially failing relational goals must still be handled deliberately.
902: 
903: Invalid or suspicious:
904: 
905: ```cosmos
906: function wait()
907:     io.read(x)
908:     x="halt"
909:     print("halted")
910: ```
911: 
912: because:
913: 
914: ```text
915: x="halt"
916: ```
917: 
918: is an ordinary relational/semidet constraint.
919: 
920: Valid:
921: 
922: ```cosmos
923: function wait()
924:     io.read(x)
925: 
926:     if(x="halt")
927:         os.halt()
928: ```
929: 
930: The `if` consumes the possible failure of the equality.
931: 
932: The `void` calls do not participate in this relational failure analysis.
933: 
934: ---
935: 
936: ## protocols
937: 
938: A protocol uses the existing declaration/type machinery.
939: 
940: Example:
941: 
942: ```cosmos
943: protocol(Moving,{
944:     Number x
945: 
946:     Relation In In move
947:     Relation Number Number move
948: })
949: ```
950: 
951: This requires:
952: 
953: ```text
954: x : Number
955: 
956: move:
957:     mode  (In, In)
958:     type  (Number, Number)
959: ```
960: 
961: No new protocol-only signature syntax is required.
962: 
963: The equivalent inline relation form is:
964: 
965: ```cosmos
966: protocol(Moving,{
967:     Number x
968: 
969:     rel move(In Number dx, In Number dy)
970:         true
971: })
972: ```
973: 
974: A relation declaration in a protocol may therefore combine:
975: 
976: - relation existence;
977: - parameter types;
978: - parameter modes;
979: - optional behavioral constraint.
980: 
981: ---
982: 
983: ## protocol relation bodies
984: 
985: Inside a protocol:
986: 
987: ```cosmos
988: rel move(In Number dx, In Number dy)
989:     true
990: ```
991: 
992: the body is a constraint/specification, not the implementation supplied to the object.
993: 
994: A body of:
995: 
996: ```cosmos
997: true
998: ```
999: 
1000: means there is no additional behavioral restriction beyond the signature.
1001: 
1002: Example:
1003: 
1004: ```cosmos
1005: protocol(Moving,{
1006:     Number x
1007: 
1008:     rel p(Number x)
1009:         x>2
1010: })
1011: ```
1012: 
1013: requires a compatible `p` and specifies that successful uses of `p(x)` must satisfy:
1014: 
1015: ```text
1016: x>2
1017: ```
1018: 
1019: In debug/runtime-contract mode, the implementation may be checked against that constraint.
1020: 
1021: ---
1022: 
1023: ## Interface-only declarations
1024: 
1025: The existing declaration form may be used without executable implementation:
1026: 
1027: ```cosmos
1028: protocol(Moving,{
1029:     Number x
1030:     Relation In In move
1031:     Relation Number Number move
1032: })
1033: ```
1034: 
1035: This is a normal structural interface.
1036: 
1037: Using:
1038: 
1039: ```cosmos
1040: rel move(In Number dx, In Number dy)
1041:     true
1042: ```
1043: 
1044: is another way to express essentially the same structural requirement while using ordinary relation syntax.
1045: 
1046: A nontrivial body adds a behavioral constraint.
1047: 
1048: ---
1049: 
1050: ## `is`
1051: 
1052: ```cosmos
1053: ship is Moving
1054: ```
1055: 
1056: checks conformance with a nominal type or protocol.
1057: 
1058: Typical mode:
1059: 
1060: ```text
1061: is(In value, In type) : semidet
1062: ```
1063: 
1064: When statically known, the compiler may prove and eliminate the runtime check.
1065: 
1066: When not statically known, it may emit structural/runtime protocol checking.

1069: 
1070: ## `new`
1071: 
1072: ```cosmos
1073: ship = new Ship(1,2)
1074: ```
1075: 
1076: means:
1077: 
1078: ```text
1079: 1. require/find Ship.new
1080: 2. call Ship.new(ship,1,2)
1081: 3. type-check/bind ship as Ship
1082: ```
1083: 
1084: It does not invoke `object.create`.
1085: 
1086: It does not install prototype behavior.
1087: 
1088: `new` is therefore constructor + type information, not object creation.

1091: 
1092: ## `object.create`
1093: 
1094: `object.create` is independent from the type system.
1095: 
1096: Its essential behavior is only to create an object with prototype information.
1097: 
1098: For example:
1099: 
1100: ```cosmos
1101: ship = object.create(Ship,{x=1,y=2})
1102: ```
1103: 
1104: may create an object conceptually containing:
1105: 
1106: ```text
1107: own fields:
1108:     x=1
1109:     y=2
1110: 
1111: prototype:
1112:     Ship
1113: ```
1114: 
1115: But the prototype does not have to be a nominal type.
1116: 
1117: For example:
1118: 
1119: ```cosmos
1120: base={x=1}
1121: 
1122: obj=object.create(base,{y=2})
1123: ```
1124: 
1125: is valid even if both `base` and `obj` are typed only as `Table`.
1126: 
1127: Thus:
1128: 
1129: ```text
1130: object.create
1131:     prototype mechanism
1132: 
1133: type/protocol
1134:     static/runtime conformance mechanism
1135: ```
1136: 
1137: They may be used together, but neither depends on the other.
1138: 
1139: ---
1140: 
1141: ## Example combinations
1142: 
1143: Plain typed constructor:
1144: 
1145: ```cosmos
1146: ship = new Ship(1,2)
1147: ```
1148: 
1149: Prototype object with no special type:
1150: 
1151: ```cosmos
1152: base={x=1}
1153: obj=object.create(base,{y=2})
1154: ```
1155: 
1156: Explicitly typed prototype object:
1157: 
1158: ```cosmos
1159: Ship ship = object.create(Ship,{x=1,y=2})
1160: ```
1161: 
1162: Later protocol check:
1163: 
1164: ```cosmos
1165: if(ship is Moving)
1166:     ship.move(1,0)
1167: ```
1168: 
1169: These are separate mechanisms that can be composed as needed.
1170: 
1171: ---
1172: 
1173: ## `class` prototype declarations
1174: 
1175: ```cosmos
1176: class(Env,{
1177:     rel new(this,result)
1178:         result=this
1179: })
1180: ```
1181: 
1182: `class(Name,Table)` declares `Name` as both a nominal type name and its
1183: immutable prototype table. It does not create an instance and does not call
1184: `object.create`; its value lowering is simply `Name = Table`. Lowercase
1185: `class(...)` is accepted as a legacy spelling, while `class(...)` is canonical.
1186: 
1187: A method selected through the class value or a value statically typed with the
1188: class receives the receiver as its first hidden argument:
1189: 
1190: ```cosmos
1191: Env.new(Env value,)      // call_cl(Env.new,[Env,value])
1192: next=value.inc(1)        // call_cl(value.inc,[value,1,next])
1193: ```
1194: 
1195: For a declared class, `new Env(args...)` resolves `Env.new` and calls it with
1196: `[Env,result,args...]`. A plain constructor table remains receiverless and is
1197: called with `[result,args...]`. Prototype installation on an instance remains
1198: explicit runtime behavior supplied by the constructor or `object.create`.

50: 
51: ```text
52: Surface AST
53:    ↓
54: name + call resolution
55:    ↓
56: normalized AST
57:    ↓
58: free-variable/capture analysis
59:    ↓
60: minimal relational IR
61:    ↓
62: Prolog
63: ```
64: 
65: In particular, the AST should preserve distinctions such as unary arithmetic expression versus unary goal operator:
66: 
67: ```text
68: -x          UnaryExpr
69: not p(x)    goal operator
70: once p(x)   goal operator
71: next p(x)   iterator/temporal goal operator
72: ```
73: 
74: but the core IR should only retain distinctions that affect backend semantics.

76: **Review item — pseudo-mutation / `!x`.** The newer proposed syntax:
77: 
78: ```cosmos
79: rel p(!x)
80:     print(x) and !x += 2
81: ```
82: 
83: with a conceptual interface such as:
84: 
85: ```text
86: p(In x1, Out x2)
87: ```
88: 
89: fits the existing relational model well if it is treated as **surface sugar for state threading**, rather than introducing mutable logical variables.
90: 
91: A useful normalization would be approximately:
92: 
93: ```cosmos
94: p(!x)
95: ```
96: 
97: →
98: 
99: ```text
100: p(x_in, x_out)
101: ```
102: 
103: and:
104: 
105: ```cosmos
106: !x += 2
107: ```
108: 
109: →
110: 
111: ```text
112: x_next = x_current + 2
113: ```
114: 
115: The important specification question is not implementation syntax but **version ordering**: each pseudo-write creates a new logical version. That suggests adding a short `state-threading.md` spec before implementing many mutation operators.
116: 
117: I would avoid making `!` itself an IR concept.
118: 
119: **Optimization opportunity:** state-threading normalization can use SSA-like naming internally:
120: 
121: ```text
122: x0 → x1 → x2
123: ```
124: 
125: Then dead versions can be eliminated and adjacent updates simplified using the same normalization machinery as ordinary expressions.

# Electron Canvas

Pack the verified compiler artifacts into the browser bundles, install
dependencies, and verify the bundled SWI-Prolog WASM runtime:

```powershell
cd D:\Computer\Documents\4
make editor
make editor-start
```

Without `make`, the same steps are:

```powershell
cd D:\Computer\Documents\4
node canvas\build-assets.mjs
cd canvas
.\install.ps1
npm.cmd start
```

`build-assets.mjs` writes `cosmos-swipl-assets.js` and
`cosmos-browser-assets.js` from `compiler/` and `libs/`. It is the only step
that produces those files, and it lives here rather than in
`compiler/build.mjs` so the compiler build never writes outside `compiler/`.
`cosmos-swipl-assets.js` keys are exact SWI-WASM filenames (`/src/swi.pl`,
`/compiler-generated/parser.pl`, ...), so `cosmos-swipl-session.js` mounts
them without inferring any directory.

cosmos_trace_call(Name,Args,Goal) :-
    (nb_current(cosmos_trace_enabled,true)->
        (nb_current(cosmos_trace_depth,Depth)->true;Depth=0),
        forall(between(1,Depth,_),put_char('|')),
        format('~s(',[Name]),cosmos_trace_args(Args),writeln(')'),flush_output,
        Next is Depth+1,b_setval(cosmos_trace_depth,Next),
        call(Goal),b_setval(cosmos_trace_depth,Depth)
    ;call(Goal)).

    cosmos_trace_value(Value),

    term_to_atom(Value,Raw),atom_concat('_',Id,Raw),format('#var~w',[Id]).

    write_term(Value,[quoted(true),max_depth(8)]).

## Summary

Modes left untouched as requested. Here's what changed for the build restructure.

**1. `make` now builds the exe; editor is separate**

`all: exe` (was `compiler test clean`), plus `make editor` (builds assets, then installs Electron deps), `make editor-assets`, and `make editor-start`. `canvas/Makefile` gained an `assets` target. `make` → verified: builds `cosmos.exe`, and `cosmos.exe -q "print('ok')"` works.

**2. The HTML/canvas dependency build moved out of `compiler/`**

`compiler/build.mjs` no longer writes outside `compiler/`. The bundle generation now lives in new **`canvas/build-assets.mjs`**, producing `cosmos-swipl-assets.js` and `cosmos-browser-assets.js` with explicit virtual-path → source-path mapping, so paths are declared once rather than derived by string surgery.

A side benefit: `swiPlBase64` and `reifPlBase64` in `cosmos-browser-assets.js` were previously empty strings, so `editor.html`'s `loadCosmosRuntime` guard would have thrown. They're now populated (and the library set went 16 → 19 files).

**3. `src/swi.pl` + `reif.pl` moved to `compiler/`**

`compiler/platform/driver.pl` (×2) and `run.pl` resolve `../swi.pl`; the manifest hashes `compiler/swi.pl`/`compiler/reif.pl`. `reif.pl` is retained as a *fallback* — `ensure_loaded(reif)` prefers the SWI library and only falls back to the bundled copy, so an engine that ships `reif` ignores it. This matters: SWI 9.0.4 here has **no** `library(reif)` (verified), and `if_/3`/`memberd_t/3` are used by `libs/list.pl`, `table.pl`, `logic.pl`, `debug.pl`, `ui_canvas.pl`, so deleting it outright would break the standard libraries.

**4. Host function is separate — verified, and now regression-guarded**

`compiler/platform/runtime.pl` declares `:- multifile cosmos_host_op/3.` and calls it, but defines no clauses; implementations live in `canvas/`, `tests/`, and the packaged payload. Added a test in `tests/generic-runtime.test.mjs` asserting no `compiler/` file implements the hook, so a future visual editor can supply its own without the compiler answering host calls first.

**Two real bugs found and fixed along the way**
- `canvas/cosmos-swipl-session.js`: the `mkdir` helper's `/exist/i` message check could never match — Emscripten reports an existing directory with an errno-only error (no `message`). It was latent until the new layout made it re-hit existing dirs. Now idempotent via `mkdir` + `readdir` confirmation. I also documented that `stat`/`lookupPath`/`mkdirTree`/`analyzePath` are all unreliable in this runtime, which cost real debugging time.
- I initially rewrote the WASM test's mount dirs and broke it; restored the original `/compiler/generated` staging layout with only the runtime paths remapped.

**Test status:** `generic-runtime` (3), `space-canvas-host` (6), `space-pipeline` (1), `events` (1) all pass. `compiler.test.mjs` has one failing test — line 67, `v2 modes, state, loops, protocols…` — which **fails identically on the untouched baseline**, so it's pre-existing and unrelated. The WASM compiler test passes (confirmed in isolation, 3/3 attempts) and I fixed the regression I'd introduced there.

One note: `make` and `make test` are now independent — `make test` no longer builds the exe, and `make` no longer runs tests. If you want `make` to also verify, say so and I'll chain them.
